edge.title: The other party who is always interested
edge.setup: A broker shows you a flat. Before you've reached the lift, there's a call about another family deciding tonight, and the owner may raise the quote tomorrow. You're asked for a token amount to 'hold' it — ₹25,000, adjustable later.
edge.tell: A deadline you can't verify, created by a person paid on commission.
move: Token money is almost never genuinely refundable, whatever is said aloud. Treat it as spent.
Say: 'If it goes, it goes.' Watch what happens to the deadline — real urgency survives this; manufactured urgency dissolves.
Ask for the owner's number and talk directly. Brokers resist this precisely because the pressure lives in the gap between you.
edge.why: A broker is paid for a transaction closing, not for you choosing well. That isn't villainy, it's structure — and once you see the structure, 'another party is interested' stops reading as information and starts reading as a job being done.
edge.variants: Same shape: car dealers' 'this EMI scheme ends today', gym joining fees waived 'only this month', insurance agents' quarter-end calls.

lens.name: Opportunity cost
lens.one_line: The true price of anything is the best thing you gave up to get it.
lens.detail: ₹5 lakh in a fixed deposit isn't 'safe' in isolation — its real cost is whatever that money would have done elsewhere, against inflation. Two hours commuting costs whatever those two hours were worth. This is also the honest way to evaluate any 'free' thing: free tends to be paid in time, attention or optionality.
elsewhere: A cheap flat 25 km out, priced in hours of your life per year.
Studying one more degree versus the earnings and experience forgone.
A free app paid for with attention and data.
lens.test: Not 'can I afford this?' but 'what is the best thing I'm giving up to have it?'
lens.today: Deccan Herald's piece on the Metro points out that a ₹50 ride can become a ₹150 journey once the last mile is added, and a mobility symposium made the same case for more buses and walkable streets. The fare on the ticket is not the cost of getting to work: add the auto or cab at each end, the wait, and the minutes. Price a route by the whole door-to-door trip, and the cheaper-looking option sometimes loses.
